fields.foundation: The Brazilian Empire was founded not through conquest but by a dynastic improvisation. On 7 September 1822, on the banks of the Ipiranga River, a stream near São Paulo, the Portuguese heir and Prince Regent Pedro proclaimed Brazilian independence with the Grito do Ipiranga, and he was acclaimed Emperor Pedro I on 12 October. The context was the crisis produced by Portugal's Liberal Revolution of 1820, whose Cortes demanded the return of the royal court to Lisbon and the reduction of Brazil to its former colonial status. Pedro, who had grown up in Brazil after the court's flight from Napoleon in 1808, found these terms politically and personally unacceptable. His declaration was as much a personal calculation as a revolutionary act: by making himself Brazil's sovereign rather than Portugal's regent, he became an emperor while preserving the institutional continuity of the colonial state. The United States recognised the new state in 1824, and Britain, which had strong commercial interests in Brazil, brokered Portugal's recognition in 1825 in exchange for financial compensation. The founding decade was turbulent. The Confederation of the Equator (1824) challenged imperial authority in the north-east. Pedro I's authoritarian style, shown when he dissolved the Constituent Assembly in 1823 and imposed his own constitution in 1824, and his reliance on Portuguese-born advisers alienated the Brazilian-born elite. His ambitions in the Río de la Plata produced the costly Cisplatine War (1825–1828), which ended with the independence of Uruguay. He abdicated in April 1831 in favour of his five-year-old son, before departing for Europe to pursue his daughter's claim to the Portuguese throne, and left the empire to a regency under which it nearly broke apart. The Regency period (1831–1840) saw serial provincial revolts, including the Cabanagem in the Amazon (1835–1840), which killed an estimated 30,000 to 40,000 people, and the Farroupilha or Ragamuffin War in Rio Grande do Sul (1835–1845), in which separatists maintained an independent republic for nearly a decade. The empire survived these years less through institutional strength than through the absence of any organised alternative and the early declaration of Pedro II's majority in 1840, at the age of fourteen.
fields.socioeconomy: Over the empire's sixty-seven years the Brazilian economy shifted from the sugar-plantation model inherited from the colonial period towards a coffee economy that would dominate Brazilian economic life for more than a century. Brazil's territory included the world's largest tropical rainforest, extensive grazing lands in the south and an exceptionally productive coffee zone in the Paraíba Valley and later western São Paulo. These gave the empire a wide range of resources, but their exploitation depended on enslaved labour. Slavery was the empire's defining social institution: well over a million enslaved Africans were landed in Brazil between 1800 and the effective end of the transatlantic trade under the Eusébio de Queirós Law of 1850, and the agriculture of the most productive provinces rested on their labour. Coffee overtook sugar as Brazil's leading export by the end of the 1830s and became the main source of both the empire's prosperity and its public finances. By mid-century Brazil was producing around half of the world's coffee, and the proceeds financed the modernisation of Rio de Janeiro, the first railways, beginning with the Mauá line of 1854, and the military effort that sustained the Paraguayan War. Under Pedro II the empire's finances were generally competently managed, with a stable currency for long periods, manageable public debt and expanding investment in railways, ports and telegraphs, while from the 1870s São Paulo planters increasingly turned to subsidised European, particularly Italian, immigration. The abolition of slavery by the Lei Áurea (Golden Law) of 1888, long overdue on moral grounds, freed the remaining enslaved people without compensation to their owners or any provision for the freedpeople themselves. It dealt a severe blow to the slaveholding elite and precipitated the political crisis that ended the empire.
fields.military: The Paraguayan War (1864–1870) turned the Brazilian military from a small, poorly funded force into a professional army with a corporate identity, institutional pride and political ambitions that would eventually prove fatal to the monarchy it served. At independence Brazil possessed no substantial standing army: Pedro I depended on Portuguese-trained officers, foreign mercenaries and militia levies, and the Regency later created the National Guard (1831), a militia controlled by local landowners, to suppress the provincial rebellions of the 1830s and 1840s. The Paraguayan War changed this. Argentina and Uruguay contributed forces, but the Brazilian army and navy did the great majority of the fighting across six years of very costly campaigns against a Paraguayan resistance that fought on even as its country was devastated. The war mobilised well over 100,000 Brazilian soldiers, produced a navy of ironclads capable of forcing the river fortress of Humaitá in 1868, and created a generation of officers hardened by sustained modern combat, among them the Duke of Caxias, the war's leading Brazilian commander. Victory in 1870 confirmed Brazil as South America's leading military power. It also sent the army home with an institutional confidence and political consciousness that made it unwilling to accept subordination to civilian politicians. The positivist ideas of Auguste Comte, spread through the military schools by teachers such as Benjamin Constant Botelho de Magalhães, convinced many officers that scientific, republican government should replace the monarchy. When Marshal Deodoro da Fonseca led the coup of November 1889 with little planning and even less public mobilisation, Pedro II offered no resistance, and the army that had won the Paraguayan War quietly ended the empire that had sent it to fight.
fields.governance: The Brazilian Empire was a constitutional monarchy that combined a parliamentary framework with an unusual fourth power, the Poder Moderador, or Moderating Power, which allowed the emperor to appoint and dismiss ministers, dissolve the Chamber of Deputies and arbitrate between the other branches of government. The system derived from the constitutional theory of the French-Swiss writer Benjamin Constant, and it gave Pedro II considerable authority exercised through constitutional forms. He alternated power between the Liberal and Conservative parties, appointing cabinets according to his own reading of political conditions and then dissolving the Chamber so that elections, managed by the government, would produce a matching majority. Pedro II was well suited to the role by temperament and intellect: genuinely learned, interested in science and philosophy (he corresponded with Louis Pasteur and Henry Wadsworth Longfellow and met Alexander Graham Bell), committed to appointment on merit, and personally opposed to slavery. The administration preserved a centralised structure inherited from the colonial period, with provincial presidents appointed by the central government rather than elected, a system that provided consistency but limited local self-government. The Amazon provinces were administered with minimal infrastructure, and the north-eastern provinces suffered recurrent droughts, above all the Great Drought of 1877–1879, which killed hundreds of thousands and drove mass migration that the state lacked the resources to address. The empire's most significant institutional weakness was the succession. The heir was Princess Isabel, whose signing of the Lei Áurea in 1888 earned her the title “a Redentora” (the Redeemer) from abolitionists but alienated the former slaveholding elite, while her French husband, the Count of Eu, was widely unpopular. Pedro II's declining health and apparent indifference to the monarchy's survival left the institution without an effective defender when the coup came.
fields.impact: The Brazilian Empire preserved Brazil's territorial unity during the most dangerous period of the new state's existence, the decades after independence when regionalism, separatism and provincial revolt threatened to break Brazil into several smaller republics on the Spanish American model. The empire's centralised constitutional framework, whatever its democratic limitations, held together a territory of some 8.5 million square kilometres through the Regency rebellions, the Paraguayan War and decades of political turbulence. The Paraguayan War, though enormously costly in lives and money, established Brazil as the leading power of South America and affected the continent's later balance of power. Abolition came by gradual legislation: the Law of the Free Womb (1871), the Sexagenarian Law (1885) and finally the Lei Áurea (1888). Brazil was the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery, but it did so, however belatedly, without the civil war that scarred the United States. Imperial patronage, through bodies such as the Imperial Academy of Fine Arts (Academia Imperial de Belas Artes) and the Brazilian Historical and Geographical Institute (1838), helped found the institutions of a Brazilian national culture, and the period produced writers such as José de Alencar and the young Machado de Assis. Pedro II studied languages including Hebrew, Sanskrit and Tupi, translated poetry into Portuguese, corresponded with leading European and American scientists and writers, and promoted Brazil's participation in international exhibitions. His example of enlightened rule coloured Brazilian intellectual life long after his exile.
fields.decline: The Brazilian Empire fell because its foundations had become obsolete and its ruler had lost the will to defend it, which made its collapse perhaps one of the most resigned in imperial history. There were three structural causes, and they reinforced one another. First, the abolition of slavery by the Lei Áurea of 13 May 1888, signed by Princess Isabel as regent while Pedro II was in Europe for medical treatment, was the right moral decision but a political catastrophe for the dynasty: many planters, who had been among the monarchy's chief supporters for more than six decades, withdrew their loyalty, and no new coalition was built to replace them. Second, the military's transformation during and after the Paraguayan War had produced an officer corps steeped in positivist and republican ideas whose members increasingly saw the monarchy as an obstacle to modernisation. The so-called Military Question of the 1880s, a series of disputes over officers' right to speak publicly and over pay, promotion and civilian interference, alienated the one institution capable of defending the empire. Third, the republican movement, launched with the Republican Manifesto of 1870 and organised in the Republican Party, grew steadily through the 1880s. It offered an organised alternative that attracted many of the coffee planters of São Paulo, the empire's most economically dynamic province, who wanted political influence proportionate to their economic weight. The coup of 15 November 1889, led by Marshal Deodoro da Fonseca, was carried out with little planning, little public participation and almost no resistance; Pedro II took no counter-measures and was sent into exile in Europe two days later. The coup had little support outside a circle of officers and republican activists. Equally, almost no one rose to defend the monarchy that Pedro II had personally ruled for forty-nine years without securing its institutional future.
fields.summary: Pedro II, the last emperor of the Brazilian Empire, showed little interest in seeing the monarchy outlive him and made no effort to defend it. He died in exile in Paris in 1891, having presided over one of the most stable and constitutional governments of nineteenth-century Latin America. His personal virtues outlasted his political will to govern.
fields.teaser: Brazil's constitutional monarchy (1822–1889) was the only lasting empire in the Americas and one of 19th-century Latin America's most stable governments. It abolished slavery in 1888, only to fall to a military coup the next year.
fields.t0: Prince Pedro declared Brazil independent of Portugal in 1822 and ruled it as Emperor Pedro I.
fields.t1: Under Pedro II the monarchy held a vast country together, while coffee grown by enslaved people drove its wealth.
fields.t2: Abolition in 1888 cost it the planters' support, and an army coup ended the empire in 1889 almost unopposed.
fields.dyk: Pedro II studied languages including Hebrew, Sanskrit and Tupi, and corresponded with Louis Pasteur and Henry Wadsworth Longfellow.
